title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
This post reviews “The Option-Critic Architecture” by Pierre-Luc Bacon, Jean Harb, and Doina Precup.
In reinforcement learning, options are temporally extended actions that allow an agent to execute multiple primitive actions over time. They provide a framework for learning and planning with temporally extended behaviors.
Previous studies often focused on discovering subgoals and learning policies to achieve them. However, identifying useful subgoals can be difficult, and learning separate policies for those subgoals may require substantial data and computation.
This paper proposes an alternative approach: learning intra-option policies and termination functions directly through policy gradient methods, without requiring manually specified subgoals or additional rewards.
The key idea is to optimize the expected discounted return of the overall task rather than learning each option solely to accomplish a predefined subgoal.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
2.1 Definition of an Option
An option is represented by the following triple:
\[
\omega=(I_\omega,\pi_\omega,\beta_\omega)
\]
where:

\(I_\omega\): Initiation set
\(\pi_\omega\): Intra-option policy
\(\beta_\omega\): Termination function

The initiation set specifies the states in which an option can be initiated.
\[
I_\omega\subseteq\mathcal{S}
\]
The intra-option policy determines the probability of selecting a primitive action while executing an option.
\[
\pi_{\omega,\theta}(a\mid s)
=
P(a_t=a\mid s_t=s,\omega_t=\omega)
\]
Here, \(\theta\) represents the parameters of the intra-option policy.
The termination function determines the probability that the current option terminates upon entering a state.
\[
\beta_{\omega,\vartheta}(s)
=
P(\text{terminate }\omega\mid s)
\]
where
\[
0\leq\beta_{\omega,\vartheta}(s)\leq1
\]
and \(\vartheta\) represents the parameters of the termination function.
Thus, an option specifies where it can start, how it selects primitive actions, and when it may terminate.
In the main derivations, the paper assumes that all options are available in every state:
\[
I_\omega=\mathcal{S},
\qquad \forall\omega\in\Omega
\]
This assumption simplifies the mathematical analysis.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
2.2 Call-and-Return Execution Model
The paper adopts the call-and-return option execution model.
An agent first selects an option according to a policy over options:
\[
\omega_t\sim\pi_\Omega(\cdot\mid s_t)
\]
It then follows the selected intra-option policy:
\[
a_t\sim\pi_{\omega_t,\theta}(\cdot\mid s_t)
\]
After the environment transitions to the next state, the termination function determines whether the option should end.
If the option continues, the agent follows the same option in the next state.
If the option terminates, the agent selects another option using \(\pi_\Omega\).
Therefore, the high-level policy does not necessarily select a new option at every primitive time step.
An option can persist across multiple primitive actions.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
3.1 Option-Value Function
The option-value function is
\[
Q_\Omega(s,\omega)
=
\sum_a
\pi_{\omega,\theta}(a\mid s)
Q_U(s,\omega,a)
\]
This represents the expected discounted return when option \(\omega\) is executed in state \(s\).
The function \(Q_U\) is the value of taking a primitive action \(a\) while executing option \(\omega\):
\[
Q_U(s,\omega,a)
=
r(s,a)
+
\gamma
\sum_{s'}
P(s'\mid s,a)
U(\omega,s')
\]
where:

\(r(s,a)\): Expected immediate reward
\(\gamma\): Discount factor
\(P(s'\mid s,a)\): State transition probability
\(U(\omega,s')\): Value upon arriving at the next state

The function \(U\) is defined as
\[
\begin{aligned}
U(\omega,s')
={}&
(1-\beta_{\omega,\vartheta}(s'))
Q_\Omega(s',\omega)\\
&+
\beta_{\omega,\vartheta}(s')
V_\Omega(s')
\end{aligned}
\]
This equation is important because it accounts for both possible outcomes after reaching the next state.
If the current option continues, its value is
\[
Q_\Omega(s',\omega)
\]
If it terminates, the agent selects an option according to the policy over options, giving the value
\[
V_\Omega(s')
=
\sum_{\omega'}
\pi_\Omega(\omega'\mid s')
Q_\Omega(s',\omega')
\]
The arrival value is therefore a probability-weighted combination of continuation and termination.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
3.2 Interpretation of the Arrival Value
The distinction between \(Q_U\) and \(U\) is important.
\(Q_U(s,\omega,a)\) evaluates a primitive action in the context of the currently executing option.
In contrast, \(U(\omega,s')\) evaluates what happens after the agent reaches the next state and considers whether to continue or terminate the option.
The termination of an option does not necessarily imply the termination of the entire episode.
It only means that the current temporally extended action has ended and that another option may be selected.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
5.1 Gradient of the Option-Value Function
Recall that
\[
Q_\Omega(s,\omega)
=
\sum_a
\pi_{\omega,\theta}(a\mid s)
Q_U(s,\omega,a)
\]
Differentiating with respect to \(\theta\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\theta Q_\Omega(s,\omega)
={}&
\sum_a
\nabla_\theta\pi_{\omega,\theta}(a\mid s)
Q_U(s,\omega,a)\\
&+
\sum_a
\pi_{\omega,\theta}(a\mid s)
\nabla_\theta Q_U(s,\omega,a)
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting the Bellman equation for \(Q_U\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\theta Q_\Omega(s,\omega)
={}&
\sum_a
\nabla_\theta\pi_{\omega,\theta}(a\mid s)
Q_U(s,\omega,a)\\
&+
\gamma\sum_a\pi_{\omega,\theta}(a\mid s)
\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)
\nabla_\theta U(\omega,s')
\end{aligned}
\]
The first term represents the direct effect of changing the probability of primitive actions.
The second term represents the indirect effect on future returns.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
5.2 Intra-Option Policy Gradient Theorem
The theorem states that
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\theta Q_\Omega(s_0,\omega_0)
={}&
\sum_{s,\omega}
\mu_\Omega(s,\omega\mid s_0,\omega_0)\\
&\times
\sum_a
\nabla_\theta\pi_{\omega,\theta}(a\mid s)
Q_U(s,\omega,a)
\end{aligned}
}
\]
where
\[
\mu_\Omega(s,\omega\mid s_0,\omega_0)
=
\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}
\gamma^t
P(s_t=s,\omega_t=\omega\mid s_0,\omega_0)
\]
is the discounted occupancy measure over state-option pairs.
It measures how frequently a state-option pair is visited along trajectories, weighted by the discount factor.
The gradient therefore combines the effect of a local policy change with its discounted frequency of occurrence.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
section: 5.3 Proof of the Intra-Option Policy Gradient Theorem
text:
5.3 Proof of the Intra-Option Policy Gradient Theorem
For this derivation, the policy over options and the termination functions are held fixed with respect to \(\theta\).

Step 1. Separate the local gradient
Define
\[
g_\theta(s,\omega)
=
\sum_a
\nabla_\theta\pi_{\omega,\theta}(a\mid s)
Q_U(s,\omega,a)
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\theta Q_\Omega(s,\omega)
={}&g_\theta(s,\omega)\\
&+\gamma\sum_a
\pi_{\omega,\theta}(a\mid s)
\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)
\nabla_\theta U(\omega,s')
\end{aligned}
\]


Step 2. Differentiate the arrival value
Recall that
\[
U(\omega,s')
=
(1-\beta_\omega(s'))Q_\Omega(s',\omega)
+
\beta_\omega(s')V_\Omega(s')
\]
Since the termination function is held fixed with respect to \(\theta\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\theta U(\omega,s')
={}&
(1-\beta_\omega(s'))
\nabla_\theta Q_\Omega(s',\omega)\\
&+
\beta_\omega(s')
\sum_{\omega'}
\pi_\Omega(\omega'\mid s')
\nabla_\theta Q_\Omega(s',\omega')
\end{aligned}
\]
This means that the gradient of the arrival value can be represented as a weighted combination of gradients of future option values.


Step 3. Express the recursion
Let
\[
G_\theta(s,\omega)
=
\nabla_\theta Q_\Omega(s,\omega)
\]
and let \(T_\Omega\) denote the transition matrix over state-option pairs.
Substituting the previous equation gives
\[
G_\theta
=
g_\theta+\gamma T_\Omega G_\theta
\]
Expanding the recursion,
\[
\begin{aligned}
G_\theta
&=g_\theta+\gamma T_\Omega G_\theta\\
&=g_\theta+\gamma T_\Omega g_\theta
+\gamma^2T_\Omega^2G_\theta\\
&=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\gamma^k T_\Omega^k g_\theta
\end{aligned}
\]
The infinite expansion follows under the discounted setting and the usual boundedness conditions.


Step 4. Recover the occupancy measure
The term
\[
T_\Omega^k((s,\omega)\mid(s_0,\omega_0))
\]
represents the probability of reaching state-option pair \((s,\omega)\) after \(k\) transitions.
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
G_\theta(s_0,\omega_0)
={}&
\sum_{s,\omega}
\left[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\gamma^k
P(s_k=s,\omega_k=\omega\mid s_0,\omega_0)
\right]\\
&\times g_\theta(s,\omega)
\end{aligned}
\]
Recognizing the term in brackets as \(\mu_\Omega\) gives
\[
\boxed{
\nabla_\theta Q_\Omega(s_0,\omega_0)
=
\sum_{s,\omega}
\mu_\Omega(s,\omega\mid s_0,\omega_0)
\sum_a
\nabla_\theta\pi_{\omega,\theta}(a\mid s)
Q_U(s,\omega,a)
}
\]
This completes the derivation.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
5.4 Interpretation
The theorem allows the agent to improve primitive-action policies while considering their contributions to the overall task.
Using the log-derivative identity,
\[
\nabla_\theta\pi_{\omega,\theta}(a\mid s)
=
\pi_{\omega,\theta}(a\mid s)
\nabla_\theta\log\pi_{\omega,\theta}(a\mid s)
\]
we obtain a sample-based gradient direction proportional to
\[
\nabla_\theta
\log\pi_{\omega,\theta}(a\mid s)
Q_U(s,\omega,a)
\]
This leads to the intra-option policy update
\[
\boxed{
\theta
\leftarrow
\theta+
\alpha_\theta
\nabla_\theta
\log\pi_{\omega,\theta}(a\mid s)
Q_U(s,\omega,a)
}
\]
Thus, the intra-option policy is updated to favor primitive actions that improve expected return.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
section: 6.1 Gradient with Respect to Termination Parameters
text:
6.1 Gradient with Respect to Termination Parameters
The derivative of the option-value function with respect to \(\vartheta\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\vartheta Q_\Omega(s,\omega)
={}&
\sum_a\pi_{\omega,\theta}(a\mid s)
\sum_{s'}\gamma P(s'\mid s,a)\\
&\times\nabla_\vartheta U(\omega,s')
\end{aligned}
\]
The key quantity is therefore
\[
\nabla_\vartheta U(\omega,s')
\]
because the termination decision is evaluated after the agent reaches the next state.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
6.2 Advantage over Options
The advantage function over options is defined as
\[
\boxed{
A_\Omega(s,\omega)
=
Q_\Omega(s,\omega)-V_\Omega(s)
}
\]
This compares the value of continuing the current option with the expected value of selecting an option according to the high-level policy.
If
\[
A_\Omega(s,\omega)>0
\]
then the current option is more valuable than the high-level policy’s expected alternative.
If
\[
A_\Omega(s,\omega)<0
\]
then the current option is less valuable, making termination potentially beneficial.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
6.3 Proof of the Termination Gradient
For this derivation, the intra-option policies and the policy over options are held fixed with respect to \(\vartheta\).

Step 1. Rewrite the arrival value
Start with
\[
U(\omega,s')
=
(1-\beta_{\omega,\vartheta}(s'))
Q_\Omega(s',\omega)
+
\beta_{\omega,\vartheta}(s')
V_\Omega(s')
\]
Equivalently,
\[
U(\omega,s')
=
Q_\Omega(s',\omega)
+
\beta_{\omega,\vartheta}(s')
\left[
V_\Omega(s')-Q_\Omega(s',\omega)
\right]
\]


Step 2. Differentiate with respect to termination parameters
Applying the product rule gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\vartheta U(\omega,s')
={}&
\nabla_\vartheta Q_\Omega(s',\omega)\\
&+
\nabla_\vartheta\beta_{\omega,\vartheta}(s')
\left[
V_\Omega(s')-Q_\Omega(s',\omega)
\right]\\
&+
\beta_{\omega,\vartheta}(s')
\left[
\nabla_\vartheta V_\Omega(s')
-
\nabla_\vartheta Q_\Omega(s',\omega)
\right]
\end{aligned}
\]
Combining terms,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\vartheta U(\omega,s')
={}&
-\nabla_\vartheta\beta_{\omega,\vartheta}(s')
A_\Omega(s',\omega)\\
&+
(1-\beta_{\omega,\vartheta}(s'))
\nabla_\vartheta Q_\Omega(s',\omega)\\
&+
\beta_{\omega,\vartheta}(s')
\nabla_\vartheta V_\Omega(s')
\end{aligned}
\]
The negative advantage term appears directly from differentiating the probability of termination.
This is the main mathematical reason for the negative sign in the termination gradient theorem.


Step 3. Express future gradients recursively
The remaining two terms depend on future returns.
Substituting the Bellman equations allows us to express the gradient as
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\vartheta U(\omega,s')
={}&
-\nabla_\vartheta\beta_{\omega,\vartheta}(s')
A_\Omega(s',\omega)\\
&+
\gamma\sum_{\omega',s''}
\widetilde{P}(s'',\omega'\mid s',\omega)
\nabla_\vartheta U(\omega',s'')
\end{aligned}
\]
Here, \(\widetilde{P}\) is the transition kernel that first accounts for termination and option selection at \(s'\), and then transitions to the following state \(s''\).
It is a one-step-shifted representation of the augmented process.
Repeated substitution expands the gradient over all future state-option pairs.


Step 4. Introduce the shifted occupancy measure
Define
\[
\widetilde{\mu}_\Omega(s',\omega\mid s_1,\omega_0)
=
\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}
\gamma^t
P(s_{t+1}=s',\omega_t=\omega\mid s_1,\omega_0)
\]
Unlike the intra-option policy gradient, which uses the pairs \((s_t,\omega_t)\), the termination gradient uses the next state together with the option that was active before the termination decision.
Expanding the recursion therefore gives
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\vartheta U(\omega_0,s_1)
={}&-
\sum_{s',\omega}
\widetilde{\mu}_\Omega(s',\omega\mid s_1,\omega_0)\\
&\times
\nabla_\vartheta\beta_{\omega,\vartheta}(s')
A_\Omega(s',\omega)
\end{aligned}
}
\]
This is the Termination Gradient Theorem in the arrival-state formulation.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
6.4 Interpretation of the Termination Gradient
The termination gradient contains
\[
-\nabla_\vartheta\beta_{\omega,\vartheta}(s')
A_\Omega(s',\omega)
\]
Consider the following cases.
Case 1: Positive Advantage
\[
A_\Omega(s',\omega)>0
\]
The current option is relatively valuable. Gradient ascent generally encourages the termination probability to decrease.
Case 2: Negative Advantage
\[
A_\Omega(s',\omega)<0
\]
The current option is relatively less valuable. Gradient ascent generally encourages the termination probability to increase.
The corresponding parameter update is
\[
\boxed{
\vartheta
\leftarrow
\vartheta-
\alpha_\vartheta
\nabla_\vartheta\beta_{\omega,\vartheta}(s')
A_\Omega(s',\omega)
}
\]
The key insight is that the agent learns when to terminate based on the relative value of the current option.
The algorithm does not require explicit termination labels or predefined subgoals.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
7.1 Execution Flow
The following diagram summarizes the call-and-return execution process.





flowchart TD
    A["Current state and option"] --> B["Sample primitive action from intra-option policy"]
    B --> C["Environment transition and reward"]
    C --> D["Critic evaluates action and option values"]
    D --> E{"Does the option terminate?"}
    E -->|"No"| F["Continue current option at next state"]
    E -->|"Yes"| G["Select option using policy over options"]
    F --> B
    G --> B
    D -.-> H["Update intra-option policy and termination function"]






The agent continues executing the same option until its termination condition is satisfied.
After termination, the high-level policy can choose another option.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
8.1 One-Step Off-Policy Update Target
When the policy over options is greedy with respect to option values, the one-step update target is
\[
\begin{aligned}
g_t^{(1)}
={}&r_{t+1}\\
&+\gamma\Big[
(1-\beta_{\omega_t,\vartheta}(s_{t+1}))
Q_\Omega(s_{t+1},\omega_t)\\
&\qquad+
\beta_{\omega_t,\vartheta}(s_{t+1})
\max_{\bar{\omega}}
Q_\Omega(s_{t+1},\bar{\omega})
\Big]
\end{aligned}
\]
The first component within the brackets represents continuing the current option.
The second component represents terminating it and selecting the most valuable option.
The TD error is
\[
\delta_t
=
g_t^{(1)}
-
Q_U(s_t,\omega_t,a_t)
\]
For a terminal next state, the continuation value is set to zero.
The critic update is
\[
Q_U(s_t,\omega_t,a_t)
\leftarrow
Q_U(s_t,\omega_t,a_t)
+
\alpha\delta_t
\]

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
8.2 Actor Updates
The intra-option policy is updated using
\[
\theta
\leftarrow
\theta+
\alpha_\theta
\nabla_\theta
\log\pi_{\omega_t,\theta}(a_t\mid s_t)
Q_U(s_t,\omega_t,a_t)
\]
The termination function is updated using
\[
\vartheta
\leftarrow
\vartheta-
\alpha_\vartheta
\nabla_\vartheta
\beta_{\omega_t,\vartheta}(s_{t+1})
A_\Omega(s_{t+1},\omega_t)
\]
Thus, the two updates serve different purposes.
The intra-option policy gradient improves which action to take.
The termination gradient improves when to stop the current option.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
8.3 Simplified Pseudocode
The following is a simplified explanation of the learning procedure, rather than a direct reproduction of the paper’s algorithm.
Initialize option policies, termination functions,
the policy over options, and the critic.

For each episode:

    Observe the initial state.
    Select an initial option.

    Until the episode ends:

        1. Sample a primitive action
           from the current intra-option policy.

        2. Execute the action and observe
           the next state and reward.

        3. Calculate the TD target and TD error.

        4. Update the critic.

        5. Update the intra-option policy
           using the policy gradient.

        6. Update the termination function
           using the option advantage.

        7. If the current option terminates,
           choose an option using the
           policy over options.

        8. Continue from the next state.
The original paper presents a tabular implementation and also studies implementations with function approximation.
The authors use a two-timescale learning framework in which the critic is updated on a faster timescale than the policy and termination parameters.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
10.1 Four-Rooms Domain
The first experiment considers navigation in a four-rooms environment.
After 1,000 episodes, the goal location changes.
The purpose is to examine whether learned options can help the agent adapt to a change in the environment.
The paper reports that Option-Critic adapts faster than the compared primitive actor-critic and SARSA(0) agents in this setting.
An interesting observation is that termination probabilities tend to become higher around doorways.
This suggests that useful temporal boundaries can emerge without explicitly providing doorway states as subgoals.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
10.2 Pinball Domain
The Pinball environment has continuous state variables and requires controlling a ball through obstacles.
The experiments demonstrate that Option-Critic can learn temporally extended and specialized behaviors in this environment.
This is important because the framework is not restricted to small tabular state spaces.

title: Paper Review: The Option-Critic Architecture
text:
10.3 Arcade Learning Environment
The paper also applies Option-Critic with deep neural network function approximation to Atari environments.
This demonstrates that the architecture can be combined with nonlinear function approximation.
However, the experimental results should not be interpreted as proving that Option-Critic is universally superior to other reinforcement learning algorithms.

title: Paper Review - Market Intraday Momentum
text:
This post is a paper review of “Market Intraday Momentum” (2018) by Lei Gao, Yufeng Han, Sophia Zhengzi Li, and Guofu Zhou. This post mainly focuses on the methods used in the paper rather than the empirical results.
This paper presents the first study of market intraday time-series momentum, according to the authors.
They found that the first half-hour market return, measured from the previous day’s market close to 10:00 a.m., predicts the last half-hour market return.
They also showed that the predictability of the last half-hour return generally increases with volatility.
Therefore, the first half-hour return could be used as an indicator for predicting the last half-hour return.

title: Paper Review - Market Intraday Momentum
text:
2.1 Predictive Regression Analysis
In the predictive regression analysis, they first considered a regression of the last half-hour return on the first half-hour return.
The regression equation is
\[
\boxed{
r_{13,t}
=
\alpha+\beta r_{1,t}+\varepsilon_t
}
\]
where:

\(r_{13,t}\): Last half-hour return
\(r_{1,t}\): First half-hour return
\(\alpha\): Intercept
\(\beta\): Regression coefficient
\(\varepsilon_t\): Error term

A positive \(\beta\) indicates a positive relationship between the first and last half-hour returns.
Then, they added the twelfth half-hour return to the regression to see whether it improved the explanatory power of the first regression.
The extended regression is
\[
\boxed{
r_{13,t}
=
\alpha
+
\beta_1r_{1,t}
+
\beta_{12}r_{12,t}
+
\varepsilon_t
}
\]
The authors compared the \(R^2\) values of the two regressions.
The first regression achieved an in-sample \(R^2\) of 1.6%, while the regression using both predictors achieved an \(R^2\) of 2.6%.
This suggests that the twelfth half-hour return provides additional predictive information.
The paper also used Newey-West robust t-statistics to evaluate the statistical significance of the regression coefficients.

title: Paper Review - Market Intraday Momentum
text:
2.2 Out-of-Sample Predictability
In the out-of-sample predictability analysis, the authors conducted recursive regressions similar to the predictive regression analysis.
To forecast the last half-hour return on day \(t\), they estimated the regression coefficients using historical data available through day \(t-1\).
For the first-half-hour-only regression, the forecast is
\[
\widehat r_{13,t}
=
\widehat\alpha_{t-1}
+
\widehat\beta_{t-1}r_{1,t}
\]
The coefficients are estimated from historical data, but \(r_{1,t}\) is observed on the same day before the last half-hour begins.
When the twelfth half-hour return is added, it is also observable by 3:30 p.m., before the prediction target period begins.
The authors initially estimated the model using observations through the end of 1997 and then expanded the estimation window by one month at a time.
To evaluate predictive performance, they used the out-of-sample \(R^2\):
\[
\boxed{
R^2_{OS}
=
1-
\frac{
\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{OS}}
(r_{13,t}-\widehat r_{13,t})^2
}{
\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{OS}}
(r_{13,t}-\overline r_{13,t})^2
}
}
\]
where:

\(r_{13,t}\): Actual last half-hour return
\(\widehat r_{13,t}\): Predicted return
\(\overline r_{13,t}\): Historical-average forecast estimated through \(t-1\)
\(\mathcal{T}_{OS}\): Out-of-sample evaluation period

If
\[
R^2_{OS}>0
\]
the predictive regression outperforms the historical-average benchmark in terms of squared forecast errors.
The authors reported an out-of-sample \(R^2\) of 1.4% using only the first half-hour return and 2.0% using both predictors.
This suggests that the predictability was not limited to the in-sample analysis.

title: Paper Review - Market Intraday Momentum
text:
2.3 Financial Crisis
For the financial crisis, the authors examined intraday momentum during the 2007–2009 financial crisis.
Conventional monthly momentum strategies are known to have performed poorly during this period.
However, the authors found that the predictive ability of the first half-hour return became stronger during the crisis.
They further showed that the predictive ability of the twelfth half-hour return also became stronger.
For example, the combined regression achieved an \(R^2\) of 6.9% during the crisis, compared with 1.1% when the crisis period was excluded.
The regression using only the twelfth half-hour return achieved an \(R^2\) of 3.1% during the crisis, compared with 0.3% outside the crisis period.
Therefore, the paper provides evidence of stronger intraday predictability during the financial crisis.
This does not necessarily imply that the twelfth half-hour return became more volatile than the first half-hour return.
Rather, it means that the twelfth half-hour return became a stronger predictor of the last half-hour return.

title: Paper Review - Market Intraday Momentum
text:
2.4 Volatility and Trading Volume
The authors found that the predictability of the last half-hour return generally increased with first half-hour realized volatility.
They divided trading days into three groups based on volatility:

Low volatility
Medium volatility
High volatility

Then, they estimated the predictive regressions separately for each group.
Using both predictors, the regression produced the following results:



Volatility group
\(R^2\)




Low
0.6%


Medium
1.0%


High

This provides evidence that first half-hour momentum is more strongly related to the last half-hour return on high-volatility days.

text:
2.5 Trade Size and Liquidity
Furthermore, the authors investigated trade size and liquidity.
These are related but different concepts.

Trade Size
The authors measured the average trade size during the last half-hour as

\]
where:

\(V_{13,t}\): Trading volume in the last half-hour
\(N_{13,t}\): Number of trades in the last half-hour

They divided trading days into small- and large-trade-size groups.
The predictive ability of the first half-hour return was relatively similar across the two groups.
The authors described the twelfth half-hour return as having stronger predictive ability on large-trade-size days.

Liquidity
Next, the authors examined liquidity using the Amihud illiquidity measure.
They divided S&P 500 stocks into portfolios with low and high Amihud measures.
A high Amihud measure indicates lower liquidity.
The measure was calculated using the average ratio of absolute stock returns to dollar trading volume over the previous five trading days.

The authors suggested that predictability may be more difficult to exploit away in less liquid markets.
This means that predictable return patterns may persist because arbitrage is more difficult.
However, greater statistical predictability does not necessarily imply greater trading profitability, since lower liquidity may increase trading costs.

title: Paper Review - Market Intraday Momentum
text:
2.6 Institutional Trading
The authors also investigated the relationship between institutional trading and intraday momentum.
They analyzed institutional holdings and institutional order imbalances.
The institutional order imbalance was measured as
\[
\boxed{
OI_t
=
\frac{BV_t-SV_t}{BV_t+SV_t}
}
\]
where:

\(BV_t\): Institutional buy volume
\(SV_t\): Institutional sell volume

This is a signed measure of institutional net buying relative to total institutional trading volume.
A larger positive value indicates stronger net buying relative to selling.
It should not be confused with the absolute magnitude of the imbalance.
The authors found that the first half-hour return had relatively stable predictive ability across groups with different institutional holdings.
In contrast, the predictive ability of the twelfth half-hour return varied more substantially.
The results also showed stronger combined predictability on days with higher institutional order imbalance values.
The authors suggested that institutional trading near the market close may contribute to intraday momentum.
However, the institutional trading data did not cover all institutions, so the results should be interpreted as supporting evidence rather than definitive proof of causation.

title: Classes and Sets 2 - The algebra of classes
text:
This post is about “The algebra of classes”.
This topic mainly covers theorems that will be useful for proving. Thus, the main contents will be theorems and their proofs.

title: Classes and Sets 2 - The algebra of classes
text:
1.20 Theorem
If \(A\) and \(B\) are any classes, then


\(A \subseteq A \cup B\) and \(B \subseteq A \cup B\).


\(A \cap B \subseteq A\) and \(B \cap A \subseteq B\).


For proving, we need the relationships from the previous post: negation, conjunction, disjunction, and implication, along with their theorems. In particular, we use 1.5(i), 1.5(i)‘, 1.5(ii), and 1.5(ii)’.
By Definition 1.13, \(x\in A\cup B\) if and only if \(x\in A\lor x\in B\). By Definition 1.14, \(x\in A\cap B\) if and only if \(x\in A\land x\in B\).
Proof (i). To prove the first statement, we need to show that every element of \(A\) is also an element of \(A \cup B\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
x \in A
&\Rightarrow x \in A \lor x \in B &&\text{by 1.5(i)}\\
&\Rightarrow x \in A \cup B &&\text{by 1.13}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(A \subseteq A \cup B\) by Definition 1.10.
Similarly, for \(B \subseteq A \cup B\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
x \in B
&\Rightarrow x \in A \lor x \in B &&\text{by 1.5(i)'}\\
&\Rightarrow x \in A \cup B &&\text{by 1.13}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(B \subseteq A \cup B\) by 1.10.
Proof (ii). For the second statement, we need to show \(x \in A \cap B \Rightarrow x \in A\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
x \in A \cap B
&\Rightarrow x \in A \land x \in B &&\text{by 1.14}\\
&\Rightarrow x \in A &&\text{by 1.5(ii)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(A \cap B \subseteq A\) by 1.10.
Similarly,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x \in B \cap A
&\Rightarrow x \in B \land x \in A &&\text{by 1.14}\\
&\Rightarrow x \in B &&\text{by 1.5(ii)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(B \cap A \subseteq B\) by 1.10.
Note: The book prints \(B \cap B \subseteq B\) in 1.20(ii). This is true, but \(B \cap A \subseteq B\) gives the symmetric statement corresponding to \(A \cap B \subseteq A\).
Next, we have the following theorem.

title: Classes and Sets 2 - The algebra of classes
text:
1.21 Theorem
If \(A\) and \(B\) are classes, then


\(A \subseteq B\) if and only if \(A \cup B = B\).


\(A \subseteq B\) if and only if \(A \cap B = A\).


Proof (i). First, suppose \(A \subseteq B\). We need to show \(A \cup B = B\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
x \in A \cup B
&\Rightarrow x \in A \lor x \in B &&\text{by 1.13}\\
&\Rightarrow x \in B \lor x \in B &&\text{since } A \subseteq B\\
&\Rightarrow x \in B &&\text{by 1.8(iv)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, \(A \cup B \subseteq B\) by 1.10. Also, \(B \subseteq A \cup B\) by 1.20(i). Therefore, \(A \cup B = B\) by 1.11(iv).
Conversely, suppose \(A \cup B = B\). By 1.20(i), \(A \subseteq A \cup B\). Hence \(A \subseteq B\) by substitution (Axiom A1).
Therefore,
\[
A \subseteq B \iff A \cup B = B.
\]
Proof (ii). First, suppose \(A \subseteq B\). By 1.20(ii), \(A \cap B \subseteq A\).
For the other inclusion,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x \in A
&\Rightarrow x \in B &&\text{by 1.10}\\
&\Rightarrow x \in A \land x \in B &&\text{since }x \in A\\
&\Rightarrow x \in A \cap B &&\text{by 1.14}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, \(A \subseteq A \cap B\) by 1.10. Consequently, \(A \cap B = A\) by 1.11(iv).
Conversely, suppose \(A \cap B = A\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
x \in A
&\Rightarrow x \in A \cap B &&\text{by Axiom A1}\\
&\Rightarrow x \in A \land x \in B &&\text{by 1.14}\\
&\Rightarrow x \in B &&\text{by 1.5(ii)'}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, \(A \subseteq B\) by 1.10, and therefore
\[
A \subseteq B \iff A \cap B = A.
\]
Next, we have

title: Classes and Sets 2 - The algebra of classes
text:
1.22 Theorem (Absorption Laws)
For all classes \(A\) and \(B\),


\(A \cup (A \cap B)=A\).


\(A \cap (A \cup B)=A\).


These can be proved with the theorems we have just covered.
Proof (i). By 1.20(ii), \(A \cap B \subseteq A\); therefore, by 1.21(i),
\[
A \cup (A \cap B)=A.
\]
Proof (ii). By 1.20(i), \(A \subseteq A \cup B\); therefore, by 1.21(ii),
\[
A \cap (A \cup B)=A.
\]
Next, we have

title: Classes and Sets 2 - The algebra of classes
text:
1.23 Theorem
For every class \(A\),
\[
(A')'=A.
\]
Proof. By Definition 1.19,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x \in (A')'
&\Rightarrow x \notin A' &&\text{by 1.19}\\
&\Rightarrow x \in A &&\text{by 1.19}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Conversely,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x \in A
&\Rightarrow x \notin A' &&\text{by 1.19}\\
&\Rightarrow x \in (A')' &&\text{by 1.19}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, \((A')' \subseteq A\) and \(A \subseteq (A')'\). Therefore, \((A')'=A\) by 1.11(iv) (or Axiom A1).
Next, we have

title: Classes and Sets 2 - The algebra of classes
text:
1.24 Theorem (De Morgan’s Laws)
For all classes \(A\) and \(B\),


\((A \cup B)'=A'\cap B'\).


\((A \cap B)'=A'\cup B'\).


Proof (i). First, by 1.19, the definition of union (1.13), and the logical De Morgan’s law (Exercise 1.1, Question 2(a)),
\[
\begin{aligned}
x \in (A \cup B)'
&\Rightarrow x \notin A \cup B &&\text{by 1.19}\\
&\Rightarrow x \notin A \land x \notin B &&\text{by 1.13 and logical De Morgan's law}\\
&\Rightarrow x \in A' \land x \in B' &&\text{by 1.19}\\
&\Rightarrow x \in A'\cap B' &&\text{by 1.14}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Conversely,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x \in A'\cap B'
&\Rightarrow x \in A' \land x \in B' &&\text{by 1.14}\\
&\Rightarrow x \notin A \land x \notin B &&\text{by 1.19}\\
&\Rightarrow x \notin A \cup B &&\text{by 1.13 and logical De Morgan's law}\\
&\Rightarrow x \in (A\cup B)' &&\text{by 1.19}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \((A \cup B)'=A'\cap B'\) by Axiom A1.
Proof (ii). To prove the second one, we can use the same definitions and the logical De Morgan’s law (Exercise 1.1, Question 2(b)).
\[
\begin{aligned}
x \in (A\cap B)'
&\Leftrightarrow x \notin A\cap B &&\text{by 1.19}\\
&\Leftrightarrow \neg[(x\in A)\land(x\in B)] &&\text{by 1.14}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\notin A\lor x\notin B &&\text{by logical De Morgan's law}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\in A'\lor x\in B' &&\text{by 1.19}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\in A'\cup B' &&\text{by 1.13}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \((A \cap B)'=A'\cup B'\) by Axiom A1.
Next, we have

title: Classes and Sets 2 - The algebra of classes
text:
1.25 Theorem
For all classes \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\), the following are true.
Commutative Laws


\(A\cup B=B\cup A\).


\(A\cap B=B\cap A\).


Idempotent Laws


\(A\cup A=A\).


\(A\cap A=A\).


Associative Laws


\(A\cup(B\cup C)=(A\cup B)\cup C\).


\(A\cap(B\cap C)=(A\cap B)\cap C\).


Distributive Laws


\(A\cap(B\cup C)=(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C)\).


\(A\cup(B\cap C)=(A\cup B)\cap(A\cup C)\).


Proof (i). By the definition of union and the commutative law of disjunction,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x\in A\cup B
&\Leftrightarrow x\in A\lor x\in B &&\text{by 1.13}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\in B\lor x\in A &&\text{by 1.8(i)}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\in B\cup A &&\text{by 1.13}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(A\cup B=B\cup A\) by Axiom A1.
Proof (ii). Similarly,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x\in A\cap B
&\Leftrightarrow x\in A\land x\in B &&\text{by 1.14}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\in B\land x\in A &&\text{by 1.8(i)'}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\in B\cap A &&\text{by 1.14}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(A\cap B=B\cap A\) by Axiom A1.
Proof (iii).
\[
\begin{aligned}
x\in A\cup A
&\Leftrightarrow x\in A\lor x\in A &&\text{by 1.13}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\in A &&\text{by 1.8(iv)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(A\cup A=A\) by Axiom A1.
Proof (iv).
\[
\begin{aligned}
x\in A\cap A
&\Leftrightarrow x\in A\land x\in A &&\text{by 1.14}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\in A &&\text{by 1.8(iv)'}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(A\cap A=A\) by Axiom A1.
Proof (v). By the definition of union and associativity of disjunction,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x\in A\cup(B\cup C)
&\Leftrightarrow x\in A\lor x\in B\cup C &&\text{by 1.13}\\
&\Leftrightarrow (x\in A)\lor[(x\in B)\lor(x\in C)] &&\text{by 1.13}\\
&\Leftrightarrow [(x\in A)\lor(x\in B)]\lor(x\in C) &&\text{by 1.8(ii)}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\in A\cup B\lor x\in C &&\text{by 1.13}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\in(A\cup B)\cup C &&\text{by 1.13}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(A\cup(B\cup C)=(A\cup B)\cup C\) by Axiom A1.
Proof (vi). Similarly, by associativity of conjunction,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x\in A\cap(B\cap C)
&\Leftrightarrow (x\in A)\land[x\in B\cap C] &&\text{by 1.14}\\
&\Leftrightarrow (x\in A)\land[(x\in B)\land(x\in C)] &&\text{by 1.14}\\
&\Leftrightarrow [(x\in A)\land(x\in B)]\land(x\in C) &&\text{by 1.8(ii)'}\\
&\Leftrightarrow [x\in A\cap B]\land(x\in C) &&\text{by 1.14}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\in(A\cap B)\cap C &&\text{by 1.14}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(A\cap(B\cap C)=(A\cap B)\cap C\) by Axiom A1.
Proof (vii). Using the distributive law of conjunction over disjunction,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x\in A\cap(B\cup C)
&\Leftrightarrow (x\in A)\land[x\in B\cup C] &&\text{by 1.14}\\
&\Leftrightarrow (x\in A)\land[(x\in B)\lor(x\in C)] &&\text{by 1.13}\\
&\Leftrightarrow [(x\in A)\land(x\in B)]\lor[(x\in A)\land(x\in C)] &&\text{by 1.8(iii)}\\
&\Leftrightarrow [x\in A\cap B]\lor[x\in A\cap C] &&\text{by 1.14}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\in(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C) &&\text{by 1.13}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(A\cap(B\cup C)=(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C)\) by Axiom A1.
Proof (viii). Using the distributive law of disjunction over conjunction,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x\in A\cup(B\cap C)
&\Leftrightarrow (x\in A)\lor[x\in B\cap C] &&\text{by 1.13}\\
&\Leftrightarrow (x\in A)\lor[(x\in B)\land(x\in C)] &&\text{by 1.14}\\
&\Leftrightarrow [(x\in A)\lor(x\in B)]\land[(x\in A)\lor(x\in C)] &&\text{by 1.8(iii)'}\\
&\Leftrightarrow [x\in A\cup B]\land[x\in A\cup C] &&\text{by 1.13}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\in(A\cup B)\cap(A\cup C) &&\text{by 1.14}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(A\cup(B\cap C)=(A\cup B)\cap(A\cup C)\) by Axiom A1.
Next, we have

title: Classes and Sets 2 - The algebra of classes
text:
1.26 Theorem
For every class \(A\), where \(\mathcal U\) is the universal class and \(\varnothing\) is the empty class,


\(A\cup\varnothing=A\).


\(A\cap\varnothing=\varnothing\).


\(A\cup\mathcal U=\mathcal U\).


\(A\cap\mathcal U=A\).


\(\mathcal U'=\varnothing\).


\(\varnothing'=\mathcal U\).


\(A\cup A'=\mathcal U\).


\(A\cap A'=\varnothing\).


Proof (i). By 1.17(i), \(\varnothing\subseteq A\). Thus, by 1.21(i), \(\varnothing\cup A=A\). Therefore, by the commutative law 1.25(i),
\[
A\cup\varnothing=A.
\]
Proof (ii). By 1.17(i), \(\varnothing\subseteq A\). Thus, by 1.21(ii), \(\varnothing\cap A=\varnothing\). Therefore, by 1.25(ii),
\[
A\cap\varnothing=\varnothing.
\]
Proof (iii). By 1.17(ii), \(A\subseteq\mathcal U\). Therefore, by 1.21(i),
\[
A\cup\mathcal U=\mathcal U.
\]
Proof (iv). By 1.17(ii), \(A\subseteq\mathcal U\). Therefore, by 1.21(ii),
\[
A\cap\mathcal U=A.
\]
Proof (v). By the definitions of complement, universal class, and empty class,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x\in\mathcal U'
&\Leftrightarrow x\notin\mathcal U &&\text{by 1.19}\\
&\Leftrightarrow \text{false} &&\text{by 1.15}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\in\varnothing &&\text{by 1.16}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(\mathcal U'=\varnothing\) by Axiom A1.
Proof (vi).
\[
\begin{aligned}
x\in\varnothing'
&\Leftrightarrow x\notin\varnothing &&\text{by 1.19}\\
&\Leftrightarrow \text{true} &&\text{by 1.16}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\in\mathcal U &&\text{by 1.15}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(\varnothing'=\mathcal U\) by Axiom A1.
Proof (vii).
\[
\begin{aligned}
x\in A\cup A'
&\Leftrightarrow (x\in A)\lor(x\in A') &&\text{by 1.13}\\
&\Leftrightarrow (x\in A)\lor(x\notin A) &&\text{by 1.19}\\
&\Leftrightarrow \text{true} &&\text{by the law of excluded middle}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\in\mathcal U &&\text{by 1.15}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(A\cup A'=\mathcal U\) by Axiom A1.
Proof (viii).
\[
\begin{aligned}
x\in A\cap A'
&\Leftrightarrow (x\in A)\land(x\in A') &&\text{by 1.14}\\
&\Leftrightarrow (x\in A)\land(x\notin A) &&\text{by 1.19}\\
&\Leftrightarrow \text{false} &&\text{by the law of noncontradiction}\\
&\Leftrightarrow x\in\varnothing &&\text{by 1.16}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(A\cap A'=\varnothing\) by Axiom A1.

2.4 Implication
Next, we have implication, which is denoted by
\[
P \implies Q
\]
and read as “P implies Q”.
It can also be interpreted as:
“If P is true, then Q is true.”
However, this does not necessarily mean that there is a causal relationship between \(P\) and \(Q\).
In classical propositional logic, an implication is false only when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false.
In all other cases, it is true.

Therefore,
\[
P\implies Q \equiv \neg P\lor Q
\]
This equivalence shows that implication can be expressed using negation and disjunction.

Example
Consider the following statements.
\[
P: 1+1=2
\]
\[
Q: \text{Water is } H_2O
\]
Both statements are true.
Therefore,
\[
P\implies Q
\]
is true.
However, the fact that \(1+1=2\) does not cause water to be \(H_2O\).
This illustrates that logical implication does not necessarily indicate causation.
In propositional logic, implication is determined by the truth values of the statements, not by their causal relationship.

text:
3.1 Steps for Constructing a Truth Table

Step 1. Identify the Variables
Write down all the basic statements in the logical expression.
For example,
\[
P,\ Q,\ R
\]
represent three distinct propositional variables.


Step 2. Determine the Number of Rows
For \(n\) distinct propositional variables, the number of possible combinations is
\[
\boxed{2^n}
\]
For example:

2 variables: \(2^2=4\) rows
3 variables: \(2^3=8\) rows
4 variables: \(2^4=16\) rows



Step 3. Create Columns
Make a column for each propositional variable.
Add additional columns for intermediate logical operations and the final expression.


Step 4. Fill in All Combinations
List every possible combination of True (T) and False (F).
For two variables, the possible combinations are
\[
(T,T),\ (T,F),\ (F,T),\ (F,F)
\]


Step 5. Evaluate the Expression
Evaluate each intermediate operation using the logical rules introduced earlier.
Finally, determine the truth value of the complete expression.

title: Classes and Sets 1 - Building Classes
text:
This post will cover “Building Classes”.
All objects are called classes, but we have to distinguish between sets and proper classes, which are two types of classes.
There is also a notation called membership notation, which is represented as follows.
If \(x\) and \(A\) are classes, and we want to say “x is an element of A”, “x belongs to A”, or “x is in A”, then we write
\[
x \in A
\]
If \(x\) is not an element of \(A\), then we write
\[
x \notin A
\]
Definition — Element
Let \(x\) be a class. If \(x\) is an element of some class \(A\), then \(x\) is called an element.
Lowercase letters represent elements, while uppercase letters may denote either elements or classes that are not elements.
In this framework, a set is a class that can be an element of another class, whereas a proper class cannot be an element of any class.

title: Classes and Sets 1 - Building Classes
text:
1.9 Definition — Equality of Classes
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be classes.
We define \(A=B\) to mean that every class that has \(A\) as an element also has \(B\) as an element, and vice versa.
In symbols,
\[
A=B
\iff
\forall X\,
\left[
(A\in X\implies B\in X)
\land
(B\in X\implies A\in X)
\right]
\]
Equivalently,
\[
A=B
\iff
\forall X\,(A\in X\iff B\in X)
\]

title: Classes and Sets 1 - Building Classes
text:
Axiom A1 — Axiom of Extent
Two classes are equal if and only if they have exactly the same elements.
\[
\boxed{
A=B
\iff
\forall x\,
(x\in A\iff x\in B)
}
\]
This axiom is sometimes called the Axiom of Extent or Axiom of Extensionality.

title: Classes and Sets 1 - Building Classes
text:
1.10 Definition — Inclusion
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be classes.
We define \(A\subseteq B\) to mean that every element of \(A\) is also an element of \(B\).
In symbols,
\[
\boxed{
A\subseteq B
\iff
\forall x\,
(x\in A\implies x\in B)
}
\]
If \(A\subseteq B\), then we say that \(A\) is a subclass of \(B\).
We define \(A\subsetneq B\) to mean that \(A\subseteq B\) and \(A\neq B\).
\[
A\subsetneq B
\iff
(A\subseteq B)\land(A\neq B)
\]
In this case, we say that \(A\) is a strict subclass of \(B\).
If \(A\) is a subclass of \(B\) and \(A\) is a set, we call \(A\) a subset of \(B\).

title: Classes and Sets 1 - Building Classes
section: 1.11 Theorem — Properties of Equality and Inclusion
text:
1.11 Theorem — Properties of Equality and Inclusion
For all classes \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\), the following hold:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(i)}\quad & A=A\\
\text{(ii)}\quad & A=B\implies B=A\\
\text{(iii)}\quad &
(A=B\land B=C)\implies A=C\\
\text{(iv)}\quad &
(A\subseteq B\land B\subseteq A)\implies A=B\\
\text{(v)}\quad &
(A\subseteq B\land B\subseteq C)\implies A\subseteq C
\end{aligned}
\]

Proof
(i) Reflexivity
The first statement is obvious because every element of class \(A\) belongs to \(A\).
For every element \(x\),
\[
x\in A\iff x\in A
\]
Therefore, by Axiom A1,
\[
A=A
\]
(ii) Symmetry
The second statement follows from Axiom A1.
If \(A=B\), then \(A\) and \(B\) have exactly the same elements.
Thus,
\[
\forall x\,
(x\in B\iff x\in A)
\]
Therefore,
\[
B=A
\]
(iii) Transitivity of Equality
For the third statement, suppose that
\[
A=B
\quad\text{and}\quad
B=C
\]
By Axiom A1,
\[
x\in A\iff x\in B
\]
and
\[
x\in B\iff x\in C
\]
for every element \(x\).
Combining these relations gives
\[
x\in A\iff x\in C
\]
Thus, by Axiom A1,
\[
\boxed{A=C}
\]
(iv) Antisymmetry of Inclusion
For the fourth statement, suppose that
\[
A\subseteq B
\quad\text{and}\quad
B\subseteq A
\]
By the definition of inclusion,
\[
x\in A\implies x\in B
\]
and
\[
x\in B\implies x\in A
\]
Therefore,
\[
x\in A\iff x\in B
\]
By Axiom A1,
\[
\boxed{A=B}
\]
(v) Transitivity of Inclusion
For the last statement, suppose that
\[
A\subseteq B
\quad\text{and}\quad
B\subseteq C
\]
If \(x\in A\), then \(x\in B\).
Since \(B\subseteq C\), we also have \(x\in C\).
Therefore,
\[
x\in A\implies x\in C
\]
By the definition of inclusion,
\[
\boxed{A\subseteq C}
\]
This completes the proof.

title: Classes and Sets 1 - Building Classes
section: Axiom A2 — Axiom of Class Construction
text:
Axiom A2 — Axiom of Class Construction
Let \(P(x)\) be a statement about \(x\) expressed using the membership relation, logical connectives, quantifiers, brackets, and variables.
The axiom states that there exists a class \(C\) consisting of all elements \(x\) that satisfy \(P(x)\).
In symbols,
\[
\boxed{
C=\{x:P(x)\}
}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\forall x\,
(x\in C\iff P(x))
\]
Axiom A2 is called the Axiom of Class Construction.
From Axiom A2, we can infer that we can form a class of all elements that satisfy \(P(x)\), but this does not mean that we can form a class whose elements are all the classes satisfying \(P(X)\).
Why is this distinction important?
If we allow arbitrary classes to be collected as elements without restriction, logical paradoxes may arise.
For example, consider the class
\[
R=\{x:x\notin x\}
\]
This is the class of all elements that do not belong to themselves.
Now, suppose that \(R\) itself is an element.
Then we can ask whether
\[
R\in R
\]
holds.
By the definition of \(R\),
\[
R\in R
\iff
R\notin R
\]
This is a contradiction.
Therefore, \(R\) cannot be an element of any class.
In this framework, \(R\) is a proper class, not a set.
The contradiction arises only if we incorrectly assume that this class can itself be treated as an element.
Thus, the distinction between elements and arbitrary classes is essential for avoiding Russell’s paradox.

title: Classes and Sets 1 - Building Classes
text:
1.12 Remark — Class Notation
The use of lowercase \(x\) in the expression
\[
C=\{x:P(x)\}
\]
is not accidental.
Lowercase letters such as \(x\) and \(y\) represent elements, whereas uppercase letters such as \(A\) and \(B\) can represent arbitrary classes.
Therefore, the expression means that \(C\) is the class of all elements \(x\) satisfying \(P(x)\).
It does not assert that \(C\) contains every arbitrary class satisfying the property.

title: Classes and Sets 1 - Building Classes
text:
1.13 Definition — Union
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be classes.
The union of \(A\) and \(B\) is the class of all elements that belong to \(A\), \(B\), or both.
In symbols,
\[
\boxed{
A\cup B
=
\{x:x\in A\lor x\in B\}
}
\]
Thus,
\[
x\in A\cup B
\iff
(x\in A\lor x\in B)
\]

title: Classes and Sets 1 - Building Classes
text:
1.14 Definition — Intersection
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be classes.
The intersection of \(A\) and \(B\) is the class of all elements that belong to both \(A\) and \(B\).
In symbols,
\[
\boxed{
A\cap B
=
\{x:x\in A\land x\in B\}
}
\]
Thus,
\[
x\in A\cap B
\iff
(x\in A\land x\in B)
\]

title: Classes and Sets 1 - Building Classes
text:
1.15 Definition — Universal Class
The universal class \(\mathcal{U}\) is the class of all elements.
In symbols,
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal{U}
=
\{x:x=x\}
}
\]
By Theorem 1.11(i),
\[
x=x
\]
holds for every element \(x\).
Therefore, every element belongs to the universal class.
\[
\forall x,\quad x\in\mathcal{U}
\]
Its existence follows from the Axiom of Class Construction.

title: Classes and Sets 1 - Building Classes
text:
1.16 Definition — Empty Class
The empty class \(\varnothing\) is the class that has no elements.
In symbols,
\[
\boxed{
\varnothing
=
\{x:x\neq x\}
}
\]
By Theorem 1.11(i),
\[
x=x
\]
for every element \(x\).
Therefore, no element can satisfy \(x\neq x\).
Hence,
\[
\forall x,\quad x\notin\varnothing
\]
The existence of the empty class also follows from the Axiom of Class Construction.

title: Classes and Sets 1 - Building Classes
text:
1.17 Theorem — Empty and Universal Classes
For every class \(A\), the following hold:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{(i)}\quad&\varnothing\subseteq A\\
\text{(ii)}\quad&A\subseteq\mathcal{U}
\end{aligned}
}
\]

Proof
(i)
In order to prove that
\[
\varnothing\subseteq A
\]
we must show that
\[
x\in\varnothing\implies x\in A
\]
for every element \(x\).
However, the empty class has no elements.
Therefore, the antecedent \(x\in\varnothing\) is always false.
An implication with a false antecedent is true, so
\[
x\in\varnothing\implies x\in A
\]
holds for every element \(x\).
Thus,
\[
\boxed{\varnothing\subseteq A}
\]
(ii)
If \(x\in A\), then \(x\) is an element.
By the definition of the universal class, every element belongs to \(\mathcal{U}\).
Therefore,
\[
x\in A\implies x\in\mathcal{U}
\]
Thus,
\[
\boxed{A\subseteq\mathcal{U}}
\]
This completes the proof.

title: Classes and Sets 1 - Building Classes
text:
1.18 Definition — Disjoint Classes
If two classes have no elements in common, they are said to be disjoint.
In symbols,
\[
\boxed{
A\cap B=\varnothing
}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\neg\exists x\,
(x\in A\land x\in B)
\]

title: Classes and Sets 1 - Building Classes
text:
1.19 Definition — Complement
The complement of a class \(A\) is the class of all elements that do not belong to \(A\).
In symbols,
\[
\boxed{
A'=\{x:x\notin A\}
}
\]
Thus,
\[
x\in A'
\iff
x\notin A
\]
Since the complement is taken with respect to the universal class, we can also write
\[
A'=\mathcal{U}\setminus A
\]

title: Exponential Moving Average (EMA)
text:
This post will cover the Exponential Moving Average (EMA), a technical indicator used to identify stock price trends and find potential buy or sell signals.
The equation for the Exponential Moving Average is as follows:
\[
EMA_t = \alpha P_t + (1-\alpha)EMA_{t-1}
\]
The equation consists of three components: the current price, the smoothing factor, and the previous period’s EMA.
Where:
The smoothing factor decreases as the number of periods increases, while the weights assigned to older prices decrease exponentially over time.
The smoothing factor is calculated as follows:
\[
\alpha = \frac{2}{N+1}
\]
where \(N\) represents the number of periods.
If we want to place less emphasis on previous values, we can increase the smoothing factor.
EMA is also used in other technical indicators and for intraday trading. EMA is useful because it assigns greater weights to recent data, which helps reduce the impact of time lags compared to a Simple Moving Average (SMA) with the same period. Thus, EMA can respond more quickly to price changes than a simple moving average.
However, there are limitations to EMA. The first limitation is that recent trends are not necessarily more important than older ones. Therefore, if recent price movements do not reflect the underlying market trend, EMA may generate false signals.
Another limitation is that EMA relies on historical data. Like all other moving averages, it is calculated using past prices. Under the Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH), market prices are assumed to reflect available information, meaning that historical price data alone may not reliably predict future price movements. Therefore, it is not advisable to rely solely on EMA; instead, it should be used in combination with other technical indicators or alpha factors.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Reinforcement Learning
text:
This post is about some of the most fundamental concepts in Reinforcement Learning: on-policy, off-policy, model-based, model-free learning, and policy gradients.
I will explain these concepts not only in words but also through equations and proofs.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Reinforcement Learning
text:
1.1 On-Policy: SARSA
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q(s_t,a_t)\leftarrow Q(s_t,a_t)+\alpha\Big[
&r_{t+1}\\
&+\gamma Q(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})\\
&-Q(s_t,a_t)
\Big]
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Fundamental Concepts of Reinforcement Learning
text:
1.2 Off-Policy: Q-Learning
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q(s_t,a_t)\leftarrow Q(s_t,a_t)+\alpha\Big[
&r_{t+1}\\
&+\gamma\max_{a}Q(s_{t+1},a)\\
&-Q(s_t,a_t)
\Big]
\end{aligned}
\]
The first equation is the on-policy SARSA update, and the second is the off-policy Q-learning update.
The main difference between these two equations is how they calculate the target for the future Q-value.
SARSA uses the next action actually selected by the current behavior policy.
In contrast, Q-learning uses the maximum estimated Q-value at the next state, regardless of which action the behavior policy actually chooses.
More technically, on-policy learning evaluates or improves the same policy that generates the agent’s behavior.
Therefore, its behavior policy and target policy are the same.
In contrast, off-policy learning can learn about a target policy using data generated by a different behavior policy.
For example, in Q-learning, the behavior policy may choose exploratory actions, while the update target uses the greedy action’s estimated value.
Thus, the behavior policy does not necessarily have to choose the same action as the target policy.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Reinforcement Learning
text:
1.3 Advantages and Limitations
Then, what is the advantage of using on-policy learning?
When an agent explores the environment, on-policy methods can learn the value of the policy it actually follows, including the effects of exploration.
This can be useful when we want to evaluate and improve the agent’s actual behavior.
However, on-policy learning is not necessarily better when the state or action space is large.
Off-policy methods can also explore and may reuse experiences generated by other behavior policies, depending on the algorithm.
Therefore, neither method is universally better. Their suitability depends on the learning objective, exploration strategy, and available data.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Reinforcement Learning
text:
2.1 Value Iteration
One typical model-based method is Value Iteration.
The value function is updated using the Bellman optimality equation:
\[
\boxed{
V_{k+1}(s)
=
\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}
\left[
R(s,a)
+
\gamma
\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}
P(s'\mid s,a)V_k(s')
\right]
}
\]
After estimating the value function, we can obtain a greedy policy:
\[
\boxed{
\pi_{k+1}(s)
\in
\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}
\left[
R(s,a)
+
\gamma
\sum_{s'}
P(s'\mid s,a)V_k(s')
\right]
}
\]
The first equation calculates the value of a state by considering the immediate reward and the expected value of the next state.
It then selects the action that maximizes this value.
The updated value function is used in the next iteration.
This process is repeated until the value function converges to the optimal value function under the usual assumptions for a discounted MDP.
The optimal policy can then be obtained by selecting the action with the highest expected return.
Thus, Value Iteration primarily updates the value function using the Bellman optimality operator.
The policy is derived from the resulting value function.
This is model-based because the algorithm uses the transition probabilities and reward function to evaluate possible actions.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Reinforcement Learning
text:
2.2 Policy Iteration
Another example is Policy Iteration, which is divided into Policy Evaluation and Policy Improvement.
Unlike Value Iteration, Policy Iteration explicitly alternates between evaluating a given policy and improving that policy.

Step 1. Policy Evaluation
First, Policy Evaluation can be written as
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
V^{\pi_k}(s)
={}&R(s,\pi_k(s))\\
&+\gamma\sum_{s'}
P(s'\mid s,\pi_k(s))
V^{\pi_k}(s')
\end{aligned}
}
\]
This equation evaluates the value of each state under the given policy \(\pi_k\).
In Policy Evaluation, the policy is held fixed while its value function is calculated.
For a discounted MDP, this can be done by solving the Bellman expectation equation or by repeatedly applying its update until convergence.


Step 2. Policy Improvement
After evaluating the current policy, we calculate the Q-value of each possible action using the evaluated value function.
\[
Q^{\pi_k}(s,a)
=
R(s,a)
+
\gamma\sum_{s'}
P(s'\mid s,a)V^{\pi_k}(s')
\]
Then, we update the policy to select an action that maximizes the Q-value:
\[
\boxed{
\pi_{k+1}(s)
\in
\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}
Q^{\pi_k}(s,a)
}
\]
The new policy is evaluated again, and the process is repeated.
Thus, Policy Iteration alternates between evaluating the current policy and improving it.
This is also model-based because the model is used to calculate the value of possible future states.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Reinforcement Learning
text:
4.1 Discounted State-Visitation Measure
Let \(p_0(s_0)\) represent the initial state distribution.
The expected return can also be written as
\[
J(\theta)
=
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
p_0(s_0)V^{\pi_\theta}(s_0)\,ds_0
\]
Define the discounted state-visitation measure as
\[
\boxed{
\rho^{\pi_\theta}(s)
=
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
p_0(s_0)
\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}
\gamma^t
p_{\pi_\theta}^{(t)}(s\mid s_0)
\,ds_0
}
\]
where
\[
p_{\pi_\theta}^{(t)}(s\mid s_0)
\]
is the probability density of reaching state \(s\) after \(t\) steps from \(s_0\) while following the policy \(\pi_\theta\).
Using this measure, the expected return can be written as
\[
\boxed{
J(\theta)
=
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
\rho^{\pi_\theta}(s)
\int_{\mathcal{A}}
\pi_\theta(a\mid s)
R(s,a)\,da\,ds
}
\]
The discounted state-visitation measure represents the expected discounted frequency of visiting each state.
It is not necessarily a normalized probability distribution.
For an infinite-horizon discounted MDP, the normalized discounted state distribution can be defined as
\[
d^{\pi_\theta}(s)
=
(1-\gamma)\rho^{\pi_\theta}(s)
\]

title: Fundamental Concepts of Reinforcement Learning
Fundamental Concepts of Reinforcement Learning
section: Step 1. Express the objective using the value function
text:
Step 1. Express the objective using the value function
We begin with
\[
J(\theta)
=
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
p_0(s_0)V^{\pi_\theta}(s_0)\,ds_0
\]
Since the value function can be written in terms of the action-value function,
\[
V^{\pi_\theta}(s_0)
=
\int_{\mathcal{A}}
\pi_\theta(a_0\mid s_0)
Q^{\pi_\theta}(s_0,a_0)
\,da_0
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
J(\theta)
=
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
p_0(s_0)
\int_{\mathcal{A}}
&\pi_\theta(a_0\mid s_0)\\
&\times Q^{\pi_\theta}(s_0,a_0)
\,da_0\,ds_0
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Fundamental Concepts of Reinforcement Learning
section: Step 2. Differentiate with respect to theta
text:
Step 2. Differentiate with respect to theta
Taking the gradient gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\theta J(\theta)
=
\int_{\mathcal{S}}p_0(s_0)
\int_{\mathcal{A}}
\nabla_\theta
\Big[
&\pi_\theta(a_0\mid s_0)\\
&\times Q^{\pi_\theta}(s_0,a_0)
\Big]
\,da_0\,ds_0
\end{aligned}
\]
Applying the product rule,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\theta J(\theta)
={}&
\int_{\mathcal{S}}p_0(s_0)
\int_{\mathcal{A}}
\nabla_\theta\pi_\theta(a_0\mid s_0)
Q^{\pi_\theta}(s_0,a_0)
\,da_0\,ds_0\\
&+
\int_{\mathcal{S}}p_0(s_0)
\int_{\mathcal{A}}
\pi_\theta(a_0\mid s_0)
\nabla_\theta Q^{\pi_\theta}(s_0,a_0)
\,da_0\,ds_0
\end{aligned}
\]
The first term represents the direct effect of changing the action probabilities.
The second term represents the effect of changing the policy on future returns.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Reinforcement Learning
text:
Step 3. Expand the action-value function
The Bellman equation for the action-value function is
\[
Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)
=
R(s,a)
+
\gamma
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
P(s'\mid s,a)
V^{\pi_\theta}(s')
\,ds'
\]
Differentiating with respect to \(\theta\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\theta Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)
={}&
\nabla_\theta R(s,a)\\
&+
\gamma\int_{\mathcal{S}}
P(s'\mid s,a)
\nabla_\theta V^{\pi_\theta}(s')
\,ds'
\end{aligned}
\]
Since the immediate reward function is assumed to be independent of \(\theta\),
\[
\nabla_\theta R(s,a)=0
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
\nabla_\theta Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)
=
\gamma
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
P(s'\mid s,a)
\nabla_\theta V^{\pi_\theta}(s')
\,ds'
}
\]
This shows that the gradient of the action-value function depends on the gradients of future state values.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Reinforcement Learning
section: Step 4. Substitute into the value-function gradient
text:
Step 4. Substitute into the value-function gradient
Recall that
\[
V^{\pi_\theta}(s)
=
\int_{\mathcal{A}}
\pi_\theta(a\mid s)
Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)
\,da
\]
Differentiating and using the previous result,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\theta V^{\pi_\theta}(s)
={}&
\int_{\mathcal{A}}
\nabla_\theta\pi_\theta(a\mid s)
Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)\,da\\
&+
\gamma
\int_{\mathcal{A}}
\pi_\theta(a\mid s)
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
P(s'\mid s,a)
\nabla_\theta V^{\pi_\theta}(s')
\,ds'\,da
\end{aligned}
\]
Define
\[
g_\theta(s)
=
\int_{\mathcal{A}}
\nabla_\theta\pi_\theta(a\mid s)
Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)\,da
\]
and the policy-induced transition kernel
\[
P_{\pi_\theta}(s'\mid s)
=
\int_{\mathcal{A}}
\pi_\theta(a\mid s)
P(s'\mid s,a)\,da
\]
Then the gradient becomes
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\theta V^{\pi_\theta}(s)
={}&
g_\theta(s)\\
&+
\gamma\int_{\mathcal{S}}
P_{\pi_\theta}(s'\mid s)
\nabla_\theta V^{\pi_\theta}(s')
\,ds'
\end{aligned}
}
\]
This is a recursive expression because the gradient of the current state’s value depends on the gradients of future states’ values.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Reinforcement Learning
text:
Step 5. Expand the recursion
Substituting the same recursive expression repeatedly gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\theta V^{\pi_\theta}(s_0)
={}&
g_\theta(s_0)\\
&+
\gamma
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
P_{\pi_\theta}(s_1\mid s_0)
g_\theta(s_1)\,ds_1\\
&+
\gamma^2
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
p_{\pi_\theta}^{(2)}(s_2\mid s_0)
g_\theta(s_2)\,ds_2\\
&+\cdots
\end{aligned}
\]
Here,
\[
p_{\pi_\theta}^{(2)}(s_2\mid s_0)
=
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
P_{\pi_\theta}(s_1\mid s_0)
P_{\pi_\theta}(s_2\mid s_1)\,ds_1
\]
represents the two-step transition probability density under policy \(\pi_\theta\).
In general, the recursive expansion becomes
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\theta V^{\pi_\theta}(s_0)
=
\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}
\gamma^t
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
&p_{\pi_\theta}^{(t)}(s\mid s_0)\\
&\times g_\theta(s)\,ds
\end{aligned}
}
\]
This means that the gradient at the initial state can be expressed as the discounted sum of local policy gradients over all future states.

title: Fundamental Concepts of Reinforcement Learning
section: Step 6. Substitute into the objective gradient
text:
Step 6. Substitute into the objective gradient
Recall that
\[
\nabla_\theta J(\theta)
=
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
p_0(s_0)
\nabla_\theta V^{\pi_\theta}(s_0)
\,ds_0
\]
Substituting the recursive expansion,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\theta J(\theta)
=
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
p_0(s_0)
\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}
\gamma^t
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
&p_{\pi_\theta}^{(t)}(s\mid s_0)\\
&\times g_\theta(s)
\,ds\,ds_0
\end{aligned}
\]
Rearranging the integrals and summation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\theta J(\theta)
=
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
\Bigg[
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
p_0(s_0)
\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}
\gamma^t
p_{\pi_\theta}^{(t)}(s\mid s_0)
\,ds_0
\Bigg]
g_\theta(s)\,ds
\end{aligned}
\]
From the definition of the discounted state-visitation measure,
\[
\rho^{\pi_\theta}(s)
=
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
p_0(s_0)
\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}
\gamma^t
p_{\pi_\theta}^{(t)}(s\mid s_0)
\,ds_0
\]
we obtain
\[
\nabla_\theta J(\theta)
=
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
\rho^{\pi_\theta}(s)
g_\theta(s)\,ds
\]
Finally, substituting the definition of \(g_\theta(s)\),
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_\theta J(\theta)
=
\int_{\mathcal{S}}
\rho^{\pi_\theta}(s)
\int_{\mathcal{A}}
&\nabla_\theta\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\\
&\times Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)
\,da\,ds
\end{aligned}
}
\]
This is the Policy Gradient Theorem.
Q.E.D.
